the study of cancer families and the investigation of the causes of childhood cancer.
the study of families containing two or more children with cancer.
the study of cancer families, the identification of genetic and environmental factors in the aetiological process and with the development of methods for the detection of high risk families.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the aetiology is unknown.
there are a number of families with a genetic aetiology, a number with an environmental aetiology and many more where the aetiology is unknown.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is a familial component in 5% of all cases of childhood cancer.
there is a genetic component in the aetiological mix in some 10% of families containing two or more children with cancer.
there is a small but real genetic component in the aetiological spectrum of childhood cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the majority of children with cancer have no other affected family members, and that most families with more than one affected child do not have an obvious aetiology.
the majority of families with two or more children with cancer have no obvious genetic or environmental aetiological factors.
there are a number of families where the risk of a second child being affected is higher than expected, and that this is not necessarily due to a single gene mutation.
